/uk-news/2026/oct/22/energy-secretary-ap.headline: Burnham’s bumpy ride ahead: PM’s in-tray full of dilemmas as parliament returns
/uk-news/2026/oct/22/energy-secretary-ap.excerpt: After a relatively cheery summer in which he announced a range of eye-catching cost of living policies, Andy Burnham may find his return to parliament this week to be a rude awakening. While the new prime minister has enjoyed some success in the polls, he is faced with many of the same problems that stymied Keir Starmer and has some difficult and unpopular choices to make. North Sea oil and gas The Rosebank oilfield and the Jackdaw gasfield have been in limbo for a year after a court case ruled the consent given to drill by the previous Conservative government was unlawful. Now, it is in the hands of the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to make the quasi-judicial decision to allow the drilling to start. Burnham has promised to take a “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil and gas as the unions complain about job losses caused by Labour’s manifesto promise to end all oil and gas licences and the Iran crisis tightens supply of gas around the globe. It has been reported Burnham will direct his energy secretary to approve the Jackdaw gasfield. Industry estimates suggest the Jackdaw gasfield could supply roughly 6% of the UK’s future gas output. But this will not impact bills, as gas is sold on a global market. He is said to be less sure about allowing Rosebank, which the former energy secretary Ed Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, referred to as “climate vandalism”.
/uk-news/2026/oct/22/energy-secretary-ap.trail: Labour leader faces tough decisions on issues such as North Sea drilling, electoral reform and defence spending

/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.headline: UK economy unexpectedly grows in August despite fall in consumer spending
/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.excerpt: The UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August despite a fall in consumer spending before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor. Figures from the Office for National Statistics showed gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 0.1% that month, compared with 0.4% growth in July. That confounded a forecast by City economists of a 0.1% contraction. With less than a fortnight before Healey’s tax and spending announcement, the ONS reading represents a surprise boost given that the Middle East war is rattling the global economy and hitting British households and businesses with a surge in energy costs. After petrol and diesel prices rose and with higher energy bills hitting household spending, the ONS said the consumer-facing services sector fell by 0.3% on the month, after a decline of 0.1% in July. Despite the overall services sector showing no growth in August, the surprise headline improvement was driven by strength in manufacturing with 0.8% growth in the wider production sector, which includes manufacturing, mining and energy generation. Construction output fell by 0.2%. The largest negative contribution came from sports, amusement and recreation activities, alongside a slump in food and drink services. Analysts said the fall could be a sign of a reversal from an earlier boost from the World Cup and unusually hot weather, or could reflect households trimming their spending. The ONS said GDP over the wider three months to the end of August rose by 0.7%.
/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.trail: Latest data showing surprise 0.1% growth is boost to John Healey a fortnight before his first budget

/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.headline: Retail sales bounce back in Great Britain amid brighter signs for economy
/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.excerpt: Retail sales across Great Britain unexpectedly rose last month, the latest economic indicator to defy gloomy forecasts as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to present next month’s budget. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold rose 0.5% month on month in August, defying analyst expectations of a 0.2% fall. It marks a significant bounce back in consumer spending after a 0.5% month-on-month fall in July. The summer heatwaves fuelled increased sales of items including fans, air-conditioning units, sports merchandise and clothing in the three months to August. The unexpected sales boost is the latest positive update on the state of the economy for the government, after a surprise 0.4% increase in gross domestic product in July that was reported by the ONS last week. “August’s warm weather delayed the usual shift towards autumn purchases, but retailers successfully kept consumers spending,” said Sandra Prince, the head of corporate consumer at Lloyds. “The late bank holiday weekend and back-to-school shopping are also likely to have supported demand, with online sales among the areas seeing the biggest boost.” Across the three-month summer period sales rose 2.4% year on year, again significantly above forecasts of a 1.9% rise. Among the strongest performers were department stores, which recorded a sales rise of 1.8% month on month in August – a bounce back after a fall in July, which the ONS attributed to stock availability problems.
/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.trail: Latest data to defy economic gloom shows 0.5% rise boosted by purchases of sports items, aircon units and fans during heatwaves

/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.headline: John Lewis losses widen to £124m as shopper confidence dips
/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.excerpt: Losses at the owner of John Lewis and Waitrose widened by more than 40% in the first half of the year as it struggled with higher costs and shoppers feeling less confident about their money. The John Lewis Partnership, which operates 36 department stores and more than 300 Waitrose supermarkets, said its pre-tax loss for the six months to 1 August climbed to £124m, compared with £88m in the same period in 2025. Jason Tarry, the chair of JLP, said the first half of the year had been a “tougher market than we had planned for”. “Customers have been more cautious about spending, particularly when they replace the bigger-ticket things in their homes,” he said, citing higher interest rates, the rising cost of living and uncertainty triggered by wars around the world. Higher national insurance contributions and a series of heatwaves over the summer also drove up costs, JLP said. Tom Denyard, the boss of Waitrose, said the heat had triggered “some challenges with refrigeration and freezing”, but that the company was investing in more resilient equipment. Waitrose still outperformed John Lewis, with sales across the supermarket arm up 4% while those at the department store chain fell 2%. Overall half-year sales rose 2% to £6.3bn. The company added that it was “starting to build” a joined-up loyalty offering across the partnership. It currently offers separate John Lewis and Waitrose loyalty cards, which include free “treat” products and personalised rewards.
/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.trail: Retailer says first half was a tougher market than it expected, though Waitrose grew sales

/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.headline: JD Sports cuts £50m from profit forecast as cost of living pressures hit trainer sales
/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.excerpt: The sports fashion retailer JD has cut £50m from its profit forecast as cost of living pressures, fuelled by the US war on Iran, weighed on sales of trainers. JD Sports, which sells brands including Nike and Adidas, said widespread inflation had hit shoppers’ wallets, particularly its core young shoppers, resulting in a drop in sales across important markets such as the US, where it struggled to shift trainers and other footwear. Bosses went on to warn that the wider fall in consumer spending was likely to continue into the second half of the year. The retailer now expects lower pre-tax profits of between £700m and £800m for the full year, having previously hoped to reach £750m to £850m. The news led to a 14% drop in JD’s London-listed shares by Thursday afternoon trading, to their lowest level since May. Régis Schultz, JD’s chief executive, said: “Trading in the second quarter remained tough,” adding that the company had been forced to cut prices and offer promotions to compensate, as “our core consumer was impacted by incremental cost-of-living pressures.” The company, which runs 4,800 stores worldwide including the JD, Blacks and Millets chains in the UK, said pressures included higher fuel prices, which have been pushed up by the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has effectively stopped tankers passing through the strait of Hormuz. Overall, JD said like-for-like sales fell by 3.1% in the second quarter, with its North America operations taking the biggest hit, down by 6.8%.
/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.trail: Inflation fuelled by Iran conflict deterring shoppers, especially in the US, says high street chain

/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.headline: Consumer confidence at near two-year high as World Cup and UK holidaying lift summer spending
/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.excerpt: Consumer confidence hit its highest level in almost two years in July, according to research that indicated the closing stages of the men’s football World Cup and more people holidaying in the UK raised summer spending. A truce in the Middle East conflict in June and the arrival of a new prime minister in No 10 also gave a lift to consumers after a long period of heightened uncertainty. A long-running monthly consumer spending survey by Barclays showed that 30% of those surveyed felt confident about the strength of the UK economy in July – representing a 21-month high and a six-percentage-point improvement on June. Consumer card spending grew by 2% year on year last month, after a 1.9% increase in June, Barclays said. The bank said the study showed people felt more secure in their jobs and had more leeway to spend on non-essentials, with discretionary spending up 1.6%. Among the biggest beneficiaries were pubs, which enjoyed a 10% increase in transactions “thanks to England’s World Cup run”. It had been estimated that the tournament had brought in £150m in added sales for British pubs. Card spending at cinemas rose 2.6%, helped by the popularity of Toy Story 5 and The Odyssey – the highest grossing movie of the film-maker Christopher Nolan’s career. In line with other surveys of economic activity, the report found that the succession of heatwaves had depressed spending on airline tickets in favour of domestic holidays, which pushed up spending on UK accommodation by 2.6%.
/business/2026/oct/23/uk-consumer-confid.trail: Barclays says survey shows people feel more secure in jobs and have more leeway to spend on non-essentials

/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.headline: US workers facing deadly heat embrace tactic that targets major brands’ reputations
/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.excerpt: “It’s the kind of heat that makes you feel like you’re being dehydrated, like your skin is drying out,” said Lucas Benitez, after harvesting watermelons with his sons and wife this summer. “The heat that we had 30 years ago is not nearly the heat that we have today.” This summer was the hottest on record in the US, and most workers in fields, greenhouses and unconditioned indoor facilities still do not have heat protections on the job, putting their health at risk as the climate crisis is expected to make extreme heat more frequent and intense. Benitez began working in tomato fields in Immokalee, Florida, when he was just 16, and in the early 1990s went on to help found the Coalition of Immokalee Workers (CIW), named after the major tomato growing region in south-west Florida. Today, CIW’s Fair Food Program has some of the strongest heat protections for workers in the country, and its approach is being emulated by other groups – in the US and beyond – as federal, state and local efforts to protect people from extreme heat stall. The program’s protections were hard won after years of boycotts, hunger strikes and protests against food corporations, and now protect farm workers in dozens of crop types. The model, described as “market-based enforcement” by academics, works by targeting the reputation of the known brand-name of a company – say a fast-food retailer – to improve conditions rather than smaller entities in the supply chain.
/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.trail: Program founded by tomato pickers has some of the strongest US worker protections – and its approach is being emulated by other groups

/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.headline: How California is bracing for a winter of floods, fires and extreme storms all at once
/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.excerpt: Before this year, the US National Weather Service had never issued a September coastal flood advisory for the San Francisco Bay Area. In the past month, it has had to issue two. As flood water swallowed intersections and eroded beaches up and down the California coast last week, scientists and emergency managers warned that this is just an early signal of a coming tumultuous winter as an already exceptional El Niño continues to strengthen. It’s been called everything from “super” to “Godzilla”, as forecasters hammer home the message that conditions brewing in the Pacific Ocean could soon climb off the charts, and fuel extreme weather around the world. Tens of millions could face food insecurity, and global food prices could be pushed higher. Climate scientists have projected that by February, more than 450,000 people around the world could succumb to spikes in temperature linked to the strong El Niño. Yet more deaths will be caused by floods and droughts, wildfires and rain. More on all this, after this week’s most important reads. Essential reads Comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and sea turtles prove nature loss can be reversed, scientists say Revealed: the methane mega-leaks from UN climate summit host Turkey To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark In focus California is among the places most likely to be hit hard by the climate pattern.
/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.trail: The strongest El Niño recorded is expected to bring a cascade of hazards to a state still facing wildfire and heat risks, while budget cuts have weakened disaster response agencies

/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.headline: July 2026 was worst on record for wildfires in England, data shows
/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.excerpt: This July was the worst on record for wildfires in England, provisional data shows, with England experiencing a clear upward trend in the total number of wildfires recorded. This summer has been a stark reminder of the vulnerability of the UK to climate breakdown, after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox. Provisional government data reveals 1,354 wildfires have been recorded so far this year, with 624 of these in July alone, making 2026 the second worst year on record. July’s wildfires included a devastating fire that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station in Suffolk and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve. The summer of 2026 was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office, with 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F) recorded, smashing the previous record of 34 days. Scientists have said the record heat of 2026 has only been possible due to the climate crisis driven by fossil-fuel burning. This year also marks the first time in the data series, which runs from 2010–26, that a death has been recorded due to a wildfire. This incident involved the death of a 70-year-old man after a fire burned in fields behind Berrington Road and Castle Gardens in Chipping Campden, Gloucestershire. Last week, the Guardian revealed that the government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires.
/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.trail: Devastating blaze near Sizewell B nuclear power station in Suffolk among a record 624 wildfires in July this year

/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.headline: Revealed: Government quietly dropped plan to prepare England for wildfires
/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.excerpt: The government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires, it has been revealed. This was despite new data showing fire crews do not have the proper protective gear to tackle them. This summer has been a potent reminder of the scale of the threat posed by the climate crisis, with the UK experiencing record-breaking wildfires after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox. In the third national climate adaptation programme, published in July 2023, the Conservative government, then headed by Rishi Sunak, said it would run a wildfire risk programme in England from 2023 to 2027 so land management would be adapted for the risk. However, it has now emerged the programme was never implemented, with the current government stating the commitment “was made by the previous government but was not brought into effect”. The environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole, who obtained the information via a freedom of information request, said it was “appalling” the government “couldn’t be bothered to pay attention to wildfire risks until jolted into doing so by Britain burning this summer”. After a wildfire spread across an area including several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands in August, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, convened an emergency Cobra meeting and issued a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues, criticised as being too little too late.
/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.trail: FOI request shows wildfire risk scheme scrapped, as data highlights many fire services lack proper protective gear

/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.headline: Southern California swelters as late-season heatwave smothers region
/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.excerpt: Southern California faced scorching heatwaves this summer that made locals wonder what happened to their famed Mediterranean climate. Now, the fall is bringing heatwaves too. Friday kicked off a new round of long-duration heatwave advisories from the National Weather Service (NWS), which expects unseasonably high temperatures to linger for at least a week. Temperatures are expected to hover near 100F in downtown Los Angeles, and spike well into the triple digits farther inland, raising the risk of both heat-related illness and wildfires. “We’re expecting temperatures will run some 15-20 degrees above normal – that’s pretty significant,” said Richard Bann, a meteorologist with the NWS’s Weather Prediction Center. “Stay cool. Stay hydrated. Limit exposure to the sun.” October heatwaves are not uncommon in southern California. They’re caused by ridges of high air pressure that park themselves above the region. This year, they’re also influenced by an ongoing marine heatwave that, in turn, is driving a strong El Niño – a year of above-average surface-water temperature in the Pacific Ocean. But experts say the severity and duration of this year’s fall heatwave is extreme, and likely to become more common in the future as the climate crisis nudges global temperatures higher. “The extremely hot temperature Friday is rare,” said V Kelly Turner, a professor of geography and urban planning at UCLA.
/environment/2026/oct/23/heat-killed-sta.trail: Temperatures expected to hover around 100F in downtown LA and even hotter inland, raising concerns about wildfires

/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-d.headline: BBC seeks to subpoena Trump children and son-in-law over defamation lawsuit
/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-d.excerpt: The BBC is trying to subpoena Donald Trump’s children as it builds its defense against the president’s defamation lawsuit centered on a documentary on the January 6 insurrection. In a motion filed on Friday, the BBC sought authorization to serve Trump’s two eldest children, Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump, and son-in-law Jared Kushner, with subpoenas for testimony and their records on the events of 6 January 2021. The BBC, its lawyers wrote in court documents, is entitled to discover Trump’s “intention behind the speech and anything that bears on the impression his audience could have reasonably obtained in listening to the speech”, which includes whether Trump “gave it intentionally or otherwise; the breadth of the audience of the message and impression; and the extent of any resulting injury or harm”. Trump filed the lawsuit against the BBC in December over scenes in the 2024 BBC documentary Trump, A Second Chance?. It argued that the BBC spliced scenes from Trump’s 6 January 2021 speech so that it appeared Trump directly urged his supporters to attack the US Capitol building. Trump’s children and son-in-law have, “without question”, knowledge of several incidents that day, BBC’s lawyers wrote, , including when Trump sought to convince former vice-president Mike Pence to refuse certifying the results of the 2020 election. The BBC also said that Kushner allegedly helped to draft a statement for Trump that would have condemned the use of violence at the Capitol.
/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-d.trail: Network wants to serve Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump Jr after president sues over January 6 documentary

/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-d.headline: US federal judge halts order for Trump to turn over financial records to BBC
/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-d.excerpt: A federal judge has temporarily halted an order requiring Donald Trump to turn over detailed financial information about his business empire to the BBC as part of an ongoing libel lawsuit. US district judge Roy Altman issued the temporary pause while he considers Trump’s request to revise and narrow parts of his lawsuit against the BBC over a 2024 documentary that aired in the UK. Trump’s legal team sought to stop the discovery order that would have given the BBC access to the president’s financial records in the multibillion-dollar case. Trump has argued the BBC’s 2024 documentary about the January 6 attack harmed his business interests. Last month, a Miami-based judge ruled that Trump would have to begin producing extensive financial records by 6 August, including information covering the hundreds of businesses held by the Trump family trust. On Wednesday, Trump’s attorneys asked the court to temporarily suspend that order, arguing the BBC had demanded a “shockingly broad amount of information based on clearly political motivations”. In a four-page order signed on Wednesday and released on Thursday, Altman said Trump’s effort to remove his claims that the documentary damaged his brand and businesses could reduce the BBC’s need to obtain his financial records. Trump’s lawyers are seeking to narrow the claim to alleged reputational harm.
/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-d.trail: Judge issues temporary pause while he considers Trump’s request to revise his libel lawsuit against BBC

/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-d.headline: Trump team pushes to block court order giving BBC access to financial records
/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-d.excerpt: Donald Trump’s legal team is making an 11th-hour attempt to block a court order that would grant the BBC access to the president’s financial records, as part of his multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the British broadcaster. Trump claims that the BBC’s 2024 documentary on the January 6 attacks have damaged the president’s business interests. In July, a Miami-based judge ruled that the president would have to start handing over detailed financial records to the BBC by 6 August. The records would reveal details into the hundreds of businesses owned by the US president’s family trust. Trump’s attorneys asked the court on Wednesday to temporarily pause the enforcement of the court order, arguing the BBC had demanded a “shockingly broad amount of information based on clearly political motivations”. Trump’s lawyers also asked the court to amend their initial lawsuit to instead focus on the “reputation harm” that was caused by the documentary, which would keep necessary disclosures “proportional to the needs of the case”, the lawyers said. While it is unclear what Trump’s net worth is, recent financial disclosures showed that he had made more than $2.2bn during his first year back in office. The lawsuit against the BBC is one of Trump’s several recent attempts to wage legal battles against media outlets that publish critical coverage of him.
/us-news/2026/oct/22/trump-bbc-lawsuit-d.trail: President has sued the broadcaster for $10bn, claiming a documentary on 2021 Capitol attack led to financial harm
